channel.title: Lullable — The Sleep Library
channel.description: Quiet, true things to read at night.

item.title: The cognitive shuffle: the sleep trick for overthinkers
item.description: Imagine a series of random, unrelated things until your thinking stops making sense. The technique, the research behind it, and how to do it tonight.

item.title: The width of a horse: how the railway gauge was chosen
item.description: Most of the world's trains run 4 feet 8½ inches apart. Nobody chose that number. It was inherited from colliery carts and ratified long after it had won.

item.title: Why do podcasts keep me awake when I'm exhausted?
item.description: Podcasts are engineered to hold attention — hooks, cliffhangers, autoplay. Why that beats your exhaustion, and what kind of audio works instead.

item.title: How long should it take to fall asleep?
item.description: Ten to twenty minutes is the healthy normal — and falling asleep instantly isn't the goal. What sleep latency is, and when it's worth attention.

item.title: The weather at the bottom of the sea
item.description: There is weather at the bottom of the Mariana Trench — currents, storms of sediment, warm springs. A quiet tour of the calmest climate on Earth.

item.title: Two men on Ben Nevis, every hour, for 21 years
item.description: From 1883 to 1904, observers on Britain's highest summit took a weather reading every single hour. A story about patience, fog, and 1.5 million numbers.

item.title: What are sleep stories, and do they work?
item.description: Sleep stories are audio narratives built to be abandoned mid-listen. How they work, when they beat meditation and white noise, and what to look for.

item.title: What is low-arousal learning?
item.description: Audio engineered to sit just below the threshold of engagement — fascinating enough to hold a racing mind, calm enough to release it into sleep.

item.title: Why can't I stop thinking at night?
item.description: A racing mind at bedtime usually isn't insomnia — it's an unoccupied brain. Why silence backfires for overthinkers, and what actually works.
